pergunta: How do stock exchanges influence global geopolitics and affect the economic life of countries, including Brazil?
emUmaFrase: Stock exchanges connect national and international capital, potentially influencing economic decisions and, to some extent, political ones.
paraComecar:
The stock exchange is the organized market where shares of publicly traded companies and other securities, such as options, are traded, as described in text [0]. It can be structured as a non‑profit civil association or, more commonly today, as a joint‑stock company that seeks profit through trading services, and must maintain high ethical standards and promptly disclose the transactions carried out.

In addition to allowing the buying and selling of securities, exchanges perform essential functions for the financial system: they provide liquidity—the ease of turning an asset into cash—and enable the raising of funds through initial public offerings (IPOs) in the primary market, while the secondary market allows continuous trading of these assets. As noted in text [1], exchanges are part of a global securities market, with electronic networks that increase speed and reduce costs, but also introduce new trading forms, such as "dark pools" and alternative systems that divert part of the volume from traditional exchanges.

In Brazil, B3 (Brasil, Bolsa, Balcão) concentrates the country's equity trading and operates under the supervision of the CVM. In 2017, it was the fifth‑largest capital market in the world, with assets of 13 billion dollars, and its historical market‑value record was reached on August 29 2014, when the 328 listed companies totaled 2.595 trillion reais ([2]). The presence of offices in London and Shanghai demonstrates its insertion into the international scene, facilitating the entry of foreign investors and the dissemination of governance practices, which directly impacts the availability of capital for Brazilian companies and, consequently, economic growth and job creation.

These interconnections make exchanges instruments of geopolitics: capital flows can be used as economic pressure, sanctions can block access to capital markets, and sharp movements in global indices can influence governments' fiscal and exchange‑rate policy decisions. Thus, variations in exchanges affect not only investors but can reverberate in foreign policy, trade agreements, and even a country's social stability, including Brazil's, by altering financing costs and the confidence of economic agents.

historiaIdeia: Exchanges have evolved from medieval fairs to global hubs that connect capital and influence economies.
historia:
The word “stock exchange” acquired a commercial meaning in 1487, when merchants from Bruges (Belgium) gathered at Van der Burse’s house to buy and sell coins, bills of exchange and precious metals. This model of a physical meeting gave rise to what we now call an organized market.

In the 16th century, the model spread across Europe: in 1561 the exchanges of Antwerp and Amsterdam appeared; in 1595 those of Lyon, Bordeaux and Marseille; and, in the second half of the century, the Royal Exchange of London was created, followed by the Paris exchange in 1639. These institutions began trading not only commodities but also securities.

In the United States, the New York Stock Exchange was born on 17 May 1792, when 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement under a plane tree on Wall Street, establishing commission rules and exclusive trading among themselves. This pact marked the start of a stock market that would become the largest in the world.

In Brazil, the exchange tradition began with the creation of the São Paulo Stock Exchange (Bovespa) in 1890, as described in B3’s history. Decades later, in 1917, the Mercantile and Futures Exchange (BM&F) was founded, expanding the scope to commodity and derivative contracts.

From the 2000s onward, the Brazilian market underwent a concentration process: all national exchanges were integrated, culminating in the merger of Bovespa with BM&F on 8 May 2008, forming BM&FBOVESPA. This union aimed to improve efficiency, reduce costs and increase liquidity.

On 22 March 2017, BM&FBOVESPA merged with CETIP, creating B3 – the first stock, commodity and over‑the‑counter exchange in Latin America. On 29 August 2014, the 328 companies listed on B3 reached a market value of 2,595 trillion reais, and in 2017 B3 was the fifth‑largest capital market exchange in the world, with assets of 13 billion dollars.

comoFuncionaIdeia: A stock exchange brings together buyers and sellers of shares, generating liquidity, transparency and global economic influence.
comoFunciona:
The stock exchange is an organized market where shares and other securities are traded; it can be a non‑profit civil association or, as is more common today, a corporation that seeks profit from trading services (source [0]).

Trading takes place in continuous auctions, traditionally on a physical trading floor or, increasingly, through electronic systems that increase speed and reduce costs (source [1]). Only broker‑dealers that are members of the exchange may operate, ensuring that transactions are carried out by authorized participants.

The exchange is obliged to disclose operations quickly, broadly and in detail, maintaining high ethical standards (source [0]). In Brazil, B3 operates under self‑regulation overseen by the Securities Commission (CVM) and has offices in London and Shanghai, facilitating connections between Brazilian and foreign investors (source [2]).

When companies list their shares, they become more transparent and subject to stricter corporate governance rules; investors can assess management by share prices, which rise or fall according to performance perception (source [1] and [1] Corporate governance). This tends to improve managerial efficiency and attract capital.

As part of a global capital market, exchanges influence investment flows between countries, affecting economic policies, exchange rates and even geopolitical decisions, since large international investors can pressure governments for reforms or economic stability.
